core: A primary source is firsthand evidence created at the time of the events by someone who witnessed or took part
The main types of primary sources: written documents, artifacts and material culture, images/maps/photographs, oral histories, and quantitative records/data
How historians analyze a primary source through sourcing: who created it, when, why, and for whom (audience and purpose)
Established analysis frameworks: Library of Congress Observe/Reflect/Question and National Archives Meet/Observe/Make-sense/Use-as-evidence
Strengths and limits of primary sources: direct evidence but partial, biased, and incomplete, so historians corroborate across multiple sources
supporting: One-line contrast with secondary sources (created after the fact, interpret primary sources); good research uses both
Whether a source counts as primary is relative to the question being asked
Historiography named as the study of how historians have interpreted the past
outOfScope: Full teaching of secondary sources (owned by the sibling secondary-sources topic)
Deep treatment of bias and perspective (hand off to bias-and-perspective)
Deep treatment of evidence-and-interpretation as a reasoning process (hand off)

claims.claim: A primary source is an object or document that comes directly from the time period to which it refers, providing firsthand evidence created by a witness to or participant in the events.

Primary sources take many forms, including government documents, letters, diaries, treaties and laws, photographs, maps, artwork, artifacts and material culture, oral histories, sound and video recordings, and research data.
Historians analyze a primary source by sourcing it: identifying who created it, when and where, why it was made, and for whom (its intended audience), before using it as evidence.

The Library of Congress structures primary-source analysis as Observe, Reflect, Question; the National Archives uses a parallel four-step sequence (meet the document, observe its parts, try to make sense of it, use it as historical evidence).

Primary sources are the closest evidence to the events studied and therefore highly valuable, but any single source is partial, shaped by its creator's perspective and purpose, and incomplete, so historians corroborate across multiple sources.
A secondary source is created after the fact and interprets or analyzes primary sources; strong historical research draws on both primary and secondary sources.
Whether a work is treated as a primary source is relative to the research question: a source is primary for the time period and phenomenon it directly comes from.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which primary sources are most reliable for reconstructing the past
positions: OpenStax notes that for historians the written word has traditionally been treated as more accurate evidence for building narratives
The same text and modern practice affirm real value in oral histories, cave paintings, and archaeological artifacts, especially for preliterate societies
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as complementary: written records are one important class of evidence, but material culture and oral history are legitimate and often essential primary sources, not lesser ones.
